rows.stem: Which of the following will be the least reactive towards nucleophilic substitution reaction ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — options (A), (B) and (D) are DRAWN structures and the stem names nothing; only (C) is printed as text. Read off the page and rendered as condensed formulae plus their names (a lossless reading, not an approximation): (A) a Kekule benzene ring bearing CH2-Cl; (B) a Kekule benzene ring bearing Cl and CH3 in a PARA (1,4) relationship, confirmed at 3x zoom; (D) a PLAIN hexagon with no inner circle and no double bonds, i.e. cyclohexane, bearing Cl. The paper's own convention distinguishes the two rings consistently (inner circle / Kekule = benzene, plain = cyclohexane). Page idx 2.
rows.solution: Nucleophilic substitution needs the \(\mathrm{C-X}\) bond to break, so the question is which chloride holds its chlorine most tightly. Methyl chloride has an unhindered \(sp^3\) carbon and reacts readily. Cyclohexyl chloride is a secondary halide and also reacts, if more slowly. Benzyl chloride is the fastest of all, because the benzyl carbocation it can form is stabilised by resonance with the ring. In 4-chlorotoluene the chlorine sits directly on the ring: its lone pair is delocalised into the \(\pi\) system, so the \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond gains partial double bond character and shortens, the carbon holding it is \(sp^2\) and more electronegative, and the electron-rich ring repels an approaching nucleophile. 4-chlorotoluene is therefore the least reactive. The lesson is the general one: a halogen ON a ring behaves quite differently from a halogen one carbon away from it.

rows.stem: The intermediate formed during the slowest step involved in the dehydration of alcohol is :
rows.solution:
Dehydration of an alcohol by concentrated sulphuric acid runs in three steps. The alcohol is first protonated, which is fast and reversible. The protonated alcohol then loses a molecule of water, and this is the slow, rate-determining step because a bond is broken and a charged fragment is created; what remains is a carbocation. In the last step a base removes a proton from the neighbouring carbon to give the alkene.

So the intermediate formed during the slowest step is a carbocation. The protonated alcohol is the species that ENTERS the slow step rather than the one formed by it, and neither a carbanion nor a free radical appears anywhere on this path.

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem: The oxidation number of Co in \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]_2(SO_4)_3}\) is :
rows.solution: The sulphate ion carries \(-2\), and there are three of them, so the anions contribute \(-6\). The formula shows two complex cations balancing that, so each carries \(+3\). Inside the complex, ethane-1,2-diamine is a neutral bidentate ligand and contributes nothing to the charge, so the entire \(+3\) belongs to the metal. The oxidation number of cobalt is \(+3\).

rows.stem: According to Werner’s theory, the primary valencies of the central metal atom :

options.label: A
options.text: are satisfied by neutral molecules or negative ions.

options.label: B
options.text: are equal to its coordination number.

rows.solution: Werner distinguished two kinds of valency. The primary valency corresponds to the oxidation state of the metal, is ionisable, and is satisfied by negative ions — the ions that sit outside the coordination sphere and are released in solution. The secondary valency is the coordination number, is non-ionisable, and is satisfied by ligands, whether neutral molecules or negative ions, held inside the coordination sphere. So of the four statements only the one saying primary valencies are satisfied by negative ions is correct; the others each describe the secondary valency instead.

rows.stem: Which of the following reagent is used to distinguish between \(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2NH}\) and \(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_3N}\) ?
rows.solution: The two amines differ in one thing only: the secondary amine still has a hydrogen on nitrogen and the tertiary amine does not. Benzenesulphonyl chloride, Hinsberg's reagent, is the test built on exactly that difference. With diethylamine it gives N,N-diethylbenzenesulphonamide, in which nitrogen has no hydrogen left, so the product is insoluble in alkali and separates out. With triethylamine there is no hydrogen on nitrogen to substitute at all, so no reaction occurs. Chloroform with potassium hydroxide is the carbylamine test, which responds only to primary amines; sodium hydroxide with iodine is the iodoform test, for methyl ketones and certain alcohols; and concentrated hydrochloric acid with zinc chloride is the Lucas test, for alcohols.

rows.stem: Among the following, which is the strongest base ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — all four options are DRAWN structures and the stem names nothing. Read off the page at 2x zoom and rendered as condensed formulae plus their names (a lossless reading): every ring carries an inner circle, i.e. benzene; (A) and (C) are PARA-disubstituted, (B) and (D) are monosubstituted. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
Basicity depends on how available the lone pair on nitrogen is. In aniline, 4-methylaniline and 4-nitroaniline the nitrogen is attached directly to the ring, so its lone pair is delocalised into the \(\pi\) system and much less available to a proton. In benzylamine a \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) group stands between the nitrogen and the ring, which breaks that conjugation completely: the lone pair stays on nitrogen, and the compound behaves like an ordinary aliphatic amine.

Among the three anilines, the methyl group makes 4-methylaniline slightly more basic than aniline and the nitro group makes 4-nitroaniline much less basic. But none of them can match benzylamine, which is the strongest base here.

rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.stem: In aqueous solution, \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}\) ion converts to which of the following in alkaline medium ?
rows.solution:
Dichromate and chromate are interconvertible, and the pH decides which one you have. In alkaline medium the added hydroxide removes protons and the orange dichromate is converted to the yellow chromate:
\(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 2\mathrm{OH^-} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
Acidifying reverses it. Note that chromium stays in the \(+6\) state throughout, so this is not a redox change: \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) would require a reducing agent as well as acid, and neither \(\mathrm{CrO}\) nor \(\mathrm{CrO_3}\) is formed in aqueous alkali.

rows.stem: The boiling point of an azeotropic mixture of water and ethanol is less than that of pure water and ethanol. The mixture shows :

options.label: D
options.text: that the solution is an ideal solution.

rows.solution: A minimum boiling azeotrope is the signature of positive deviation. In a water-ethanol mixture the hydrogen bonding between an ethanol molecule and a water molecule is weaker than the hydrogen bonding each has with its own kind, so mixing loosens the liquid. More molecules escape than Raoult's law predicts, both partial vapour pressures come out too high, and the total vapour pressure is therefore raised. A mixture with a higher vapour pressure needs less heating to reach the external pressure, which is exactly why this azeotrope boils below either pure component.

rows.stem: The mole fraction of a solute in \(2{\cdot}0\) molal aqueous solution is :
rows.solution:
A 2.0 molal solution contains 2 mol of solute in 1000 g of water. The moles of water follow from its molar mass:
\(n_{\mathrm{water}} = \dfrac{1000}{18} = 55.55\ \mathrm{mol}\)

The mole fraction of the solute is then
\(x_{\text{solute}} = \dfrac{2}{2 + 55.55} = \dfrac{2}{57.55} = 0.0347\)

The most common error here is to divide by the moles of solvent alone rather than by the total, which gives 0.036 and misses the intended choice; the other distractors are that figure moved by powers of ten.

rows.stem: On electrolysis of very dilute aqueous solution of NaCl using platinum electrodes :
rows.solution:
Two things compete at each electrode, and the concentration decides the anode.

At the cathode the candidates are \(\mathrm{Na^+}\) and water. Sodium's reduction potential is far too negative for it to be deposited from aqueous solution, so water is reduced instead and hydrogen gas is evolved at the cathode.

At the anode the candidates are \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\) and water. In a concentrated solution the chloride wins on overpotential grounds and chlorine is obtained, but the question specifies a VERY DILUTE solution: there is too little chloride for it to compete, so water is oxidised and oxygen is released. That makes the statement about hydrogen at the cathode the correct one — and note that the answer about oxygen at the anode would also be true for a dilute solution, which is why the cathode statement, true at any concentration, is the safer reading of what the question is testing.

rows.stem: For a reaction \(\mathrm{3A \rightarrow 2B}\), the rate of reaction \(\dfrac{+\,\mathrm{d[B]}}{\mathrm{dt}}\) is equal to :
rows.solution:
Rates of appearance and disappearance are tied together by the stoichiometric coefficients. For \(3\mathrm{A} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{B}\) the single rate of reaction is
\(-\dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{dt} = +\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{d[\mathrm{B}]}{dt}\)

Multiplying through by 2,
\(\dfrac{d[\mathrm{B}]}{dt} = -\dfrac{2}{3}\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{dt}\)

The minus sign is not optional: \(d[\mathrm{A}]/dt\) is itself negative because A is being consumed, so the minus makes the right-hand side positive, as it must be for a species being formed.

rows.stem: On hydrolysis, which of the following carbohydrates gives only glucose ?
rows.solution: Galactose is a monosaccharide, so it does not hydrolyse at all. Sucrose hydrolyses to one glucose and one fructose, and lactose to one glucose and one galactose, so both give a second sugar alongside glucose. Maltose is built from two glucose units joined by an \(\alpha\)-1,4 glycosidic linkage, so hydrolysis gives glucose and nothing else.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Separation of Zr and Hf is difficult.
Reason (R) : Because Zr and Hf lie in the same group of the periodic table.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Zirconium and hafnium are genuinely hard to separate, so the Assertion is true. The cause is lanthanoid contraction: hafnium follows the lanthanoids, whose poorly shielding 4f electrons let the nuclear charge pull the outer shells in, and the result is that hafnium ends up almost exactly the same size as zirconium, one period above it. Nearly identical radii mean nearly identical chemistry.

Merely belonging to the same group is not the explanation. Titanium is in that group too and is easy enough to separate from either, because it is distinctly smaller. So the Assertion is true while the Reason is false.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Phenol is less acidic than 4-methylphenol.
Reason (R) : The presence of an electron releasing group in phenol makes it less acidic.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Acidity of a phenol depends on how well the phenoxide ion left behind can carry its negative charge. An electron-releasing group pushes electron density towards that charge and destabilises it, making the phenol less acidic. The methyl group of 4-methylphenol is exactly such a group, so 4-methylphenol is LESS acidic than phenol, not more.

The Reason states this principle correctly and is true. The Assertion has the comparison the wrong way round and is false. So the Assertion is false while the Reason is true.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Aromatic primary amines cannot be prepared by Gabriel phthalimide synthesis.
Reason (R) : Gabriel phthalimide synthesis is used for the preparation of primary aliphatic amines.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Gabriel phthalimide synthesis really is restricted to primary aliphatic amines, and aromatic primary amines really cannot be made by it, so both statements are true.

But the Reason only repeats the scope of the method; it does not say why the scope is what it is. The actual explanation is that the step involved is a nucleophilic substitution of the phthalimide anion on a halide, and an aryl halide will not undergo that substitution. So both statements are true but the Reason is not the explanation of the Assertion.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Order of reaction is applicable to elementary as well as complex reactions.
Reason (R) : Order of a reaction is an experimental quantity.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Order is determined from the experimentally measured rate law, and a rate law can be written for any reaction, so order is meaningful for elementary and complex reactions alike. Molecularity is the quantity that is not: it counts the molecules in a single elementary step, so a multi-step reaction has none. Both statements here are therefore true.

They are not, however, offered as cause and effect. What makes order applicable to a complex reaction is that it is read off the OVERALL rate law rather than off any mechanism; being an experimentally measured quantity is a separate fact about how order is obtained. So both are true but the Reason is not the explanation of the Assertion.

rows.stem:
For the compound having molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_4H_9Br}\), write :
(a) the isomer which is most reactive towards \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) displacement.
(b) the isomer which, on reacting with Na metal in the presence of dry ether, gives 2,5-Dimethylhexane.
rows.solution:
(a) An \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reaction goes through a carbocation, so the most reactive isomer is the one that forms the most stable cation. The tertiary halide does this best, since three alkyl groups release electron density towards the positive centre:
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{CBr}\), 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.

(b) The Wurtz reaction couples two alkyl halide units through the carbon that carried the halogen, so the product is symmetrical about that new bond. Cutting 2,5-dimethylhexane, \((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{CH-CH_2-CH_2-CH(CH_3)_2}\), down the middle gives two isobutyl fragments, so the halide must be the isobutyl one:
\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(CH_3)-CH_2-Br}\), 1-bromo-2-methylpropane.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
For a reaction \(\mathrm{A + B \rightarrow Products}\), the rate law is :
\(\text{Rate} = \mathrm{k[A][B]}^{3/2}\)
Write the overall order of the reaction. Can this reaction be an elementary reaction ? Give reason in support of your answer.
rows.solution:
The overall order is the sum of the exponents in the rate law:
\(1 + \dfrac{3}{2} = \dfrac{5}{2}\)

No, this cannot be an elementary reaction. For an elementary reaction the order must equal the molecularity, because the rate law can then be written straight from the single step. Molecularity counts the molecules that collide, so it has to be a whole number; an order of \(\tfrac{5}{2}\) cannot be matched by any molecularity, which means the reaction must proceed through more than one step.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: Explain why, on addition of 1 mol of KCl to 1 litre of water, the boiling point of water increases, while the addition of 1 mol of methyl alcohol to 1 litre of water decreases the boiling point.
rows.solution:
Both changes are colligative, and the difference is that only one of the two solutes is non-volatile.

Potassium chloride is a non-volatile electrolyte. It dissolves and dissociates into \(\mathrm{K^+}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\), so 1 mol of it puts about 2 mol of particles into the water. Those particles occupy part of the surface and lower the vapour pressure of the solution, so the liquid must be heated further before its vapour pressure matches the external pressure. The boiling point therefore rises.

Methyl alcohol is a volatile liquid, so it contributes its own vapour pressure instead of lowering the solution's. The mixture's total vapour pressure is higher than that of pure water, and the mixture also boils as a whole rather than as a solvent holding a solute, so it reaches the external pressure at a lower temperature. Methanol molecules also hydrogen bond to water in place of water's own stronger water-to-water bonds, which loosens the liquid further. The boiling point therefore falls.

rows.stem:
Write IUPAC names of the following compounds :
(i) \(\mathrm{[PtCl_2(en)_2]SO_4}\)
(ii) \(\mathrm{(NH_4)_2[CoF_4]}\)
rows.solution:
(i) The sulphate ion outside the coordination sphere carries \(-2\), so the complex cation is \(+2\). Inside it, two chlorido ligands contribute \(-2\) and the two ethane-1,2-diamine ligands are neutral, so platinum must be \(+4\). Ligands are cited alphabetically, chlorido before ethane-1,2-diamine, and since the ligand name itself contains numerals the multiplying prefix is bis. The name is dichloridobis(ethane-1,2-diamine)platinum(IV) sulphate.

(ii) Two ammonium ions outside contribute \(+2\), so the complex anion is \(-2\). Four fluorido ligands contribute \(-4\), which leaves cobalt at \(+2\). The complex is the anion, so cobalt takes the \(-ate\) ending. The name is ammonium tetrafluoridocobaltate(II).

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem:
Define the following terms with a suitable example in each case :
(i) Ambidentate ligand
(ii) Double salt
rows.solution:
(i) An ambidentate ligand is a monodentate ligand that carries two different donor atoms and can attach to the metal through either one, though only through one at a time. The nitrite ion is the standard example: it binds through nitrogen as nitrito-N, written \(\mathrm{-NO_2}\), or through oxygen as nitrito-O, written \(\mathrm{-ONO}\). The thiocyanate ion behaves the same way, binding through either sulphur or nitrogen.

(ii) A double salt is an addition compound of two simple salts in a fixed stoichiometric ratio which is stable in the solid state but dissociates completely into its simple ions when dissolved in water, so none of its original identity survives in solution. Mohr's salt, \(\mathrm{FeSO_4 \cdot (NH_4)_2SO_4 \cdot 6H_2O}\), is one example and potash alum, \(\mathrm{K_2SO_4 \cdot Al_2(SO_4)_3 \cdot 24H_2O}\), another. A complex, by contrast, keeps its coordination sphere intact in solution.

rows.stem:
How do you explain the following ?
(a) Presence of a straight chain in glucose
(b) Presence of five – OH groups in glucose which are attached to different carbon atoms
rows.solution:
(a) Glucose heated for a long time with hydriodic acid is reduced completely, every oxygen being stripped away, and what is left is \(n\)-hexane — the straight-chain hydrocarbon, not a branched isomer:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{HI},\ \Delta} \mathrm{CH_3(CH_2)_4CH_3}\)
Since the carbon skeleton cannot rearrange under these conditions, the six carbons of glucose must already have been in an unbranched chain.

(b) Glucose reacts with acetic anhydride to give a stable pentaacetate, that is a derivative in which exactly five acetyl groups have been introduced:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{(\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O}} \text{glucose pentaacetate}\)
Acetylation happens at hydroxyl groups, so there must be five of them. That they sit on five different carbons follows from the fact that the compound is stable: two hydroxyl groups on the same carbon would make a gem-diol, which loses water at once.

rows.stem:
The half-life period of a radioactive element is \(1{\cdot}5 \times 10^{10}\) years. Calculate the time in which the activity of the element is reduced to 75% of its original value.
[Given : \(\log 2 = 0{\cdot}30,\ \log 3 = 0{\cdot}48,\ \log 4 = 0{\cdot}60\)]
rows.solution:
The element is radioactive, so its decay is first order and the rate constant follows from the half-life:
\(k = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{1.5 \times 10^{10}}\ \mathrm{year^{-1}}\)

Activity is proportional to the amount left, so an activity down to 75% means 75 parts remaining out of an original 100. Using the first order equation rearranged for time,
\(t = \dfrac{2.303}{k}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]} = \dfrac{2.303 \times 1.5 \times 10^{10}}{0.693}\log\dfrac{100}{75}\)

The logarithm is handled with the values supplied, since \(\dfrac{100}{75} = \dfrac{4}{3}\):
\(\log\dfrac{4}{3} = \log 4 - \log 3 = 0.60 - 0.48 = 0.12\)

so
\(t = \dfrac{2.303 \times 1.5 \times 10^{10}}{0.693} \times 0.12 = 0.598 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{years}\)

that is about \(6 \times 10^{9}\) years.

rows.stem: State Kohlrausch’s law of independent migration of ions. With the help of a curve, explain why it is not easy to determine \(\Lambda_m^{o}\) for weak electrolytes by extrapolating the concentration – molar conductivity curve, as it is for strong electrolytes.
rows.solution:
Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions states that at infinite dilution, where the ions are so far apart that they no longer influence one another, the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the sum of the individual limiting contributions of its cation and its anion, each weighted by how many of them the formula unit provides.

Now plot molar conductivity against the square root of concentration for each type of electrolyte.

For a strong electrolyte the plot is very nearly a straight line over the dilute range. It slopes gently downwards as concentration rises, because the electrolyte is already fully dissociated and the only change is increasing interionic attraction, which slows the ions a little. A straight line can be produced backwards to \(\sqrt{C} = 0\), and its intercept on the vertical axis gives \(\Lambda^{\circ}_m\) directly.

For a weak electrolyte the plot is a curve. At ordinary concentrations only a small fraction of the molecules is dissociated, so the conductivity is low; as the solution is diluted the degree of dissociation climbs steeply towards 1, and the curve rises sharply and runs almost parallel to the vertical axis near the origin instead of meeting it at a definite point. There is no straight portion to extrapolate, so \(\Lambda^{\circ}_m\) cannot be read off the graph and must be obtained indirectly — by adding the limiting ionic conductivities, which is what Kohlrausch's law makes possible.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: An antifreeze solution is prepared by dissolving 31 g of ethylene glycol (Molar mass = \(62\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)) in 600 g of water. Calculate the freezing point of the solution. (\(\mathrm{K_f}\) for water = \(1{\cdot}86\ \mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}}\))
rows.solution:
The freezing point depression is
\(\Delta T_f = K_f \times \dfrac{W_B}{M_B} \times \dfrac{1000}{W_A}\)

With \(K_f = 1.86\) K kg \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\), \(W_B = 31\) g, \(M_B = 62\) g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\) and \(W_A = 600\) g,
\(\Delta T_f = 1.86 \times \dfrac{31}{62} \times \dfrac{1000}{600} = 1.55\ \mathrm{K}\)

The depression is subtracted from the freezing point of the pure solvent, and for water that is \(0\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\):
\(T_f = T_f^{\circ} - \Delta T_f = 0 - 1.55 = -1.55\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)

which is \(273.15 - 1.55 = 271.6\ \mathrm{K}\). Ethylene glycol is non-volatile and does not dissociate, so no van't Hoff factor enters — which is precisely what makes it a good antifreeze.

rows.stem:
Answer the following questions about the complexes \(\mathrm{[NiCl_4]^{2-}}\) and \(\mathrm{[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}}\) :
(i) Write the hybridization involved in each case.
(ii) Which of them is the inner orbital complex and which one is the outer orbital complex ?
(iii) Compare their magnetic behaviour.
[Atomic number : Ni = 28]
rows.solution:
Nickel is \(+2\) in both complexes, so \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) is \(3d^8\) in both; the ligands decide the rest.

(i) The chloride ion is a weak field ligand and does not disturb the \(3d^8\) arrangement, so bonding uses the outer \(4s\) and \(4p\) orbitals: \(\mathrm{[NiCl_4]^{2-}}\) is \(sp^3\) hybridised. Cyanide is a strong field ligand and forces the two unpaired \(3d\) electrons to pair, freeing one \(3d\) orbital for bonding: \(\mathrm{[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}}\) is \(dsp^2\) hybridised.

(ii) The names follow from which d orbitals are used. \(\mathrm{[NiCl_4]^{2-}}\) uses no inner d orbital, so it is an outer orbital complex; \(\mathrm{[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}}\) uses an inner \(3d\) orbital, so it is an inner orbital complex.

(iii) \(\mathrm{[NiCl_4]^{2-}}\) keeps its two unpaired electrons and is paramagnetic. \(\mathrm{[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}}\) has none left unpaired and is diamagnetic. The geometries differ too: the first is tetrahedral, the second square planar.

rows.subtopic: Importance and Applications of Coordination Compounds
rows.stem:
(i) Name two coordination compounds which are important in biological systems.
(ii) What is meant by chelate effect ? Give an example.
(iii) Why are low spin tetrahedral complexes rarely formed ?
rows.solution:
(i) Haemoglobin, the iron complex that carries oxygen in blood, and chlorophyll, the magnesium complex that captures light in green plants. Vitamin \(\mathrm{B_{12}}\), a cobalt complex, and the zinc enzymes carboxypeptidase A and carbonic anhydrase are equally good answers.

(ii) The chelate effect is the extra stability a complex gains when a bidentate or polydentate ligand binds the same metal ion through two or more donor atoms, closing a ring. \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]^{3+}}\), in which three ethane-1,2-diamine molecules each close a five-membered ring with the cobalt, is far more stable than \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\) with six separate ammonia ligands.

(iii) A low spin complex forms only when the crystal field splitting energy exceeds the energy needed to pair two electrons in one orbital. In a tetrahedral field only four ligands approach the metal, and none of them head-on along an orbital axis, so the splitting \(\Delta_t\) is small — about four-ninths of the octahedral value for the same ligands. \(\Delta_t\) is therefore almost always less than the pairing energy, the electrons stay unpaired, and low spin tetrahedral complexes are rarely formed.

rows.stem:
Give reasons for the following :
(a) Although chlorine is an electron-withdrawing group, yet it is ortho-, para-directing in electrophilic aromatic substitution reactions.
(b) Aryl halides cannot be prepared by reacting phenol with concentrated halogen acids or phosphorus halides.
(c) Chloroform is stored in closed dark coloured bottles.
rows.solution:
(a) The two effects of chlorine pull in opposite directions and act on different questions. Chlorine is more electronegative than carbon, so its \(-I\) effect withdraws electron density from the whole ring and makes chlorobenzene react more slowly than benzene: that is why it is called deactivating. But chlorine also carries lone pairs, and its \(+R\) effect donates one of them into the ring, building up electron density specifically at the ortho and para positions. When an electrophile attacks there, the resulting carbocation intermediate has an extra resonance structure in which chlorine's lone pair carries the positive charge, and no such structure exists for meta attack. So the rate is lowered overall by \(-I\) but the position is chosen by \(+R\): chlorine is deactivating and ortho, para directing at the same time.

(b) The bond that would have to break is the carbon-oxygen bond of the phenol, and in a phenol that bond is not an ordinary single bond. The oxygen lone pair is delocalised into the ring, so the \(\mathrm{C-O}\) bond acquires partial double bond character and is both shorter and stronger than in an alcohol. Neither a concentrated halogen acid nor a phosphorus halide can break it, so the halide is never introduced and the reaction simply fails.

(c) Chloroform is slowly oxidised by the oxygen of the air in the presence of light to phosgene, \(\mathrm{COCl_2}\), which is extremely poisonous:
\(2\mathrm{CHCl_3} + \mathrm{O_2} \xrightarrow{\text{light}} 2\mathrm{COCl_2} + 2\mathrm{HCl}\)
Dark coloured glass keeps the light out and a closely filled, closed bottle keeps the air out, so both requirements of the reaction are denied.

rows.stem:
How will you obtain the following from benzenediazonium chloride ? Give chemical equations involved :
(a) Chlorobenzene
(b) Benzene
(c) Benzonitrile
rows.solution:
All three are replacements of the diazonium group, which leaves as nitrogen gas — the reason diazonium salts are so useful in synthesis.

(a) Chlorobenzene, by the Sandmeyer reaction. Warming the diazonium salt with cuprous chloride in hydrochloric acid replaces the group by chlorine:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Cu_2Cl_2}/\mathrm{HCl}} \mathrm{C_6H_5Cl} + \mathrm{N_2}\)

(b) Benzene, by reduction. Hypophosphorous acid with water, or ethanol, supplies a hydrogen atom in place of the diazonium group:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-} + \mathrm{H_3PO_2} + \mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_6} + \mathrm{N_2} + \mathrm{H_3PO_3} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

(c) Benzonitrile, again by the Sandmeyer reaction but with cuprous cyanide:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{CuCN}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CN} + \mathrm{N_2}\)

rows.stem: An organic compound (A) with molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_3H_5N}\) on reaction with \(\mathrm{C_6H_5MgBr}\) followed by hydrolysis, gives a compound (B). Compound (B) forms an orange-red precipitate with 2,4-DNP reagent and does not give iodoform test. It neither reduces Tollens’ or Fehling’s reagent nor does it decolourise bromine water. On drastic oxidation with chromic acid it gives a carboxylic acid (C) having molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_7H_6O_2}\). Identify the compounds (A), (B) and (C). Write the reactions of compound (A) with \(\mathrm{C_6H_5MgBr}\) followed by hydrolysis to give compound (B).
rows.solution:
The formula \(\mathrm{C_3H_5N}\) with three carbons and a nitrogen, reacting with a Grignard reagent, points to a nitrile, and the only one with three carbons is propanenitrile:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CN}\)

A Grignard reagent adds across the carbon-nitrogen triple bond, and hydrolysis of the adduct gives a ketone, so B is the ketone from the propyl fragment and the phenyl group:
\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CN} + \mathrm{C_6H_5MgBr} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H^+}]{\mathrm{H_2O}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-CO-CH_2-CH_3}\)
so \(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_2CH_3}\), 1-phenylpropan-1-one.

Every one of the tests fits. The orange-red precipitate with 2,4-DNP confirms a carbonyl group. No iodoform test means the carbonyl does not carry a methyl group, which rules out phenyl methyl ketone and fixes the ethyl side. Failing to reduce Tollens' or Fehling's reagent confirms a ketone rather than an aldehyde. Not decolourising bromine water rules out any carbon-carbon double bond.

Drastic oxidation with chromic acid burns the whole side chain back to a single carboxyl carbon on the ring, and \(\mathrm{C_7H_6O_2}\) is benzoic acid:
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}\)

rows.stem: Write the name of basic building units of proteins and nucleic acids. How can you differentiate between Fibrous and Globular proteins on the basis of their structures ?
rows.context: Living systems are made up of various complex biomolecules like carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, etc. Proteins and carbohydrates are essential constituents of our food. In addition, some simple molecules like vitamins and mineral salts also play an important role in the functions of organisms. All proteins are polymers of \(\alpha\)-amino acids. Proteins can be classified into two types on the basis of their molecular shape — Fibrous and Globular proteins. Vitamins are accessory food factors required in the diet. They are classified as fat-soluble and water-soluble. Deficiency of vitamins leads to many diseases. Nucleic acids are the polymers of nucleotides which in turn consist of a base, a pentose sugar and phosphate moiety. There are two types of nucleic acids — DNA and RNA. Nucleic acids are responsible for the transfer of characters from parents to offsprings.
rows.solution:
The basic building unit of a protein is the \(\alpha\)-amino acid; residues are joined through peptide linkages into polypeptide chains. The basic building unit of a nucleic acid is the nucleotide, each made of a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and a phosphate group.

The two classes of protein differ in how the chains are arranged. In a fibrous protein the polypeptide chains lie parallel to one another and are held side by side by hydrogen bonds and disulphide bridges, giving a thread-like structure that is insoluble in water; keratin and myosin are examples. In a globular protein the chain coils and folds back on itself into a roughly spherical shape, and these are generally soluble in water; insulin and albumin are examples.

rows.stem: What products would be formed when a nucleotide from DNA containing thymine is hydrolyzed ?
rows.context: Living systems are made up of various complex biomolecules like carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, etc. Proteins and carbohydrates are essential constituents of our food. In addition, some simple molecules like vitamins and mineral salts also play an important role in the functions of organisms. All proteins are polymers of \(\alpha\)-amino acids. Proteins can be classified into two types on the basis of their molecular shape — Fibrous and Globular proteins. Vitamins are accessory food factors required in the diet. They are classified as fat-soluble and water-soluble. Deficiency of vitamins leads to many diseases. Nucleic acids are the polymers of nucleotides which in turn consist of a base, a pentose sugar and phosphate moiety. There are two types of nucleic acids — DNA and RNA. Nucleic acids are responsible for the transfer of characters from parents to offsprings.
rows.solution: Hydrolysis breaks a nucleotide into its three components. A DNA nucleotide containing thymine therefore gives the base thymine, the pentose sugar 2-deoxy-D-ribose, and phosphoric acid. Partial hydrolysis would stop one step earlier, at the nucleoside thymidine plus phosphoric acid.

rows.stem: Write one structural difference between DNA and RNA.
rows.context: Living systems are made up of various complex biomolecules like carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, etc. Proteins and carbohydrates are essential constituents of our food. In addition, some simple molecules like vitamins and mineral salts also play an important role in the functions of organisms. All proteins are polymers of \(\alpha\)-amino acids. Proteins can be classified into two types on the basis of their molecular shape — Fibrous and Globular proteins. Vitamins are accessory food factors required in the diet. They are classified as fat-soluble and water-soluble. Deficiency of vitamins leads to many diseases. Nucleic acids are the polymers of nucleotides which in turn consist of a base, a pentose sugar and phosphate moiety. There are two types of nucleic acids — DNA and RNA. Nucleic acids are responsible for the transfer of characters from parents to offsprings.
rows.solution: DNA is double stranded, two polynucleotide chains coiled about each other in a double helix and held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, whereas RNA is normally a single strand. The sugar differs too: DNA carries 2-deoxy-D-ribose and RNA carries D-ribose; and DNA uses thymine where RNA uses uracil.

rows.stem:
Name the reagents used in the following reactions :
(i) Oxidation of a primary alcohol to aldehyde
(ii) Oxidation of a primary alcohol to carboxylic acid
rows.context: Alcohols have higher boiling points than other compounds, namely hydrocarbons, ethers and haloalkanes of comparable molecular masses. On oxidation, primary alcohols yield aldehydes with mild oxidizing agents and carboxylic acids with strong oxidizing agents. Secondary alcohols yield ketones on oxidation while tertiary alcohols are resistant to oxidation. Ethers may be prepared by dehydration of alcohols and Williamson synthesis. The C – O bond in ethers can be cleaved by hydrogen halides. The presence of – OH group in phenols activates the aromatic ring towards electrophilic substitution and directs the incoming group to ortho and para positions due to resonance effect. In presence of NaOH, phenol generates phenoxide ion which is even more reactive than phenol. Thus, in alkaline medium, phenol undergoes Kolbe’s reaction.
rows.solution:
(i) A mild oxidising agent is needed, one that stops at the aldehyde instead of carrying on to the acid, and it must work without water present. Pyridinium chlorochromate, \(\mathrm{CrO_3}\) in pyridine and hydrochloric acid, does this. Chromium trioxide itself in a non-aqueous medium serves the same purpose.

(ii) A strong oxidising agent is wanted here, so acidified potassium permanganate is used; acidified potassium dichromate does the job equally well. These carry the oxidation through the aldehyde stage to the carboxylic acid without stopping.

rows.stem: Write the reaction involved in Kolbe’s reaction.
rows.context: Alcohols have higher boiling points than other compounds, namely hydrocarbons, ethers and haloalkanes of comparable molecular masses. On oxidation, primary alcohols yield aldehydes with mild oxidizing agents and carboxylic acids with strong oxidizing agents. Secondary alcohols yield ketones on oxidation while tertiary alcohols are resistant to oxidation. Ethers may be prepared by dehydration of alcohols and Williamson synthesis. The C – O bond in ethers can be cleaved by hydrogen halides. The presence of – OH group in phenols activates the aromatic ring towards electrophilic substitution and directs the incoming group to ortho and para positions due to resonance effect. In presence of NaOH, phenol generates phenoxide ion which is even more reactive than phenol. Thus, in alkaline medium, phenol undergoes Kolbe’s reaction.
rows.solution:
Kolbe's reaction converts phenol into salicylic acid. Phenol is first treated with aqueous sodium hydroxide to give sodium phenoxide, which is a stronger nucleophile than phenol itself. Carbon dioxide is then passed in and attacks the ring ortho to the oxygen, and acidification of the product gives 2-hydroxybenzoic acid:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} \xrightarrow{\text{aq. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5O^-Na^+} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H^+}]{\mathrm{CO_2}} \text{2-hydroxybenzoic acid}\)

rows.stem: Why are tertiary alcohols resistant to oxidation ?
rows.context: Alcohols have higher boiling points than other compounds, namely hydrocarbons, ethers and haloalkanes of comparable molecular masses. On oxidation, primary alcohols yield aldehydes with mild oxidizing agents and carboxylic acids with strong oxidizing agents. Secondary alcohols yield ketones on oxidation while tertiary alcohols are resistant to oxidation. Ethers may be prepared by dehydration of alcohols and Williamson synthesis. The C – O bond in ethers can be cleaved by hydrogen halides. The presence of – OH group in phenols activates the aromatic ring towards electrophilic substitution and directs the incoming group to ortho and para positions due to resonance effect. In presence of NaOH, phenol generates phenoxide ion which is even more reactive than phenol. Thus, in alkaline medium, phenol undergoes Kolbe’s reaction.
rows.solution: Oxidation of an alcohol proceeds by removing the hydrogen on the carbon that carries the \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group, together with the hydrogen of the \(-\mathrm{OH}\) itself, and forming a carbon-oxygen double bond in their place. A tertiary alcohol has no hydrogen at all on that carbon — all three of its other valencies are taken by alkyl groups — so the double bond cannot be formed and the alcohol resists oxidation. Under drastic conditions it can be attacked, but only by breaking carbon-carbon bonds, which gives a mixture of smaller fragments rather than a clean product.

rows.stem:
Write the products of the following reaction :
\(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-O-C_2H_5} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{HI}}\)
rows.context: Alcohols have higher boiling points than other compounds, namely hydrocarbons, ethers and haloalkanes of comparable molecular masses. On oxidation, primary alcohols yield aldehydes with mild oxidizing agents and carboxylic acids with strong oxidizing agents. Secondary alcohols yield ketones on oxidation while tertiary alcohols are resistant to oxidation. Ethers may be prepared by dehydration of alcohols and Williamson synthesis. The C – O bond in ethers can be cleaved by hydrogen halides. The presence of – OH group in phenols activates the aromatic ring towards electrophilic substitution and directs the incoming group to ortho and para positions due to resonance effect. In presence of NaOH, phenol generates phenoxide ion which is even more reactive than phenol. Thus, in alkaline medium, phenol undergoes Kolbe’s reaction.
rows.solution:
Cleavage of an ether by hydrogen iodide gives an alcohol and an alkyl iodide, and which fragment gets the iodine depends on the groups present. Here one group is tertiary, so the reaction takes the unimolecular route: the protonated ether breaks to give the relatively stable tertiary carbocation, which the iodide ion then captures. The iodine therefore attaches to the tertiary carbon:
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C-O-C_2H_5} + \mathrm{HI} \longrightarrow (\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C-I} + \mathrm{C_2H_5OH}\)
The products are 2-iodo-2-methylpropane and ethanol. Had both groups been primary, the mechanism would have been bimolecular and the iodide would have attacked the less hindered carbon instead.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
(i) Describe giving reason which one of the following pairs has the property indicated :
(I) Fe or Cu – higher melting point
(II) \(\mathrm{Ti^{3+}}\) or \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\) – coloured in aqueous solution
(III) Cr or Zn – higher third ionisation enthalpy
(ii) Write the ionic equations for the oxidizing action of \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\) in acidic medium with :
(I) \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) ion
(II) \(\mathrm{I^-}\) ion
rows.solution:
(i)(I) Iron has the higher melting point. The strength of metallic bonding depends on how many unpaired d electrons each atom can contribute to it. Iron is \(3d^6 4s^2\) and has four unpaired d electrons available; copper is \(3d^{10} 4s^1\), its d subshell completely filled and paired, so only the single \(4s\) electron takes part. Weaker metallic bonding means the lower melting point for copper.

(II) \(\mathrm{Ti^{3+}}\) is coloured in aqueous solution. Colour in these ions comes from a d-d transition, which needs a partly filled d subshell. \(\mathrm{Ti^{3+}}\) is \(3d^1\) and has one electron to promote, so it absorbs visible light and appears purple. \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\) is \(3d^0\), with no d electron at all, so no d-d transition is possible and the solution is colourless.

(III) Zinc has the higher third ionisation enthalpy. The third electron must come from a \(\mathrm{M^{2+}}\) ion, and for zinc that ion is \(3d^{10}\) — a completely filled, particularly stable subshell that gives up an electron only with difficulty. For chromium the corresponding ion is \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\), \(3d^4\), and losing one more electron actually improves matters by producing the half-filled-adjacent \(3d^3\) arrangement.

(ii)(I) Permanganate oxidises iron(II) to iron(III) and is itself reduced to \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\):
\(\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 5\mathrm{Fe^{2+}} + 8\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 5\mathrm{Fe^{3+}} + 4\mathrm{H_2O}\)

(II) With iodide in acid it goes to iodine:
\(2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 10\mathrm{I^-} + 16\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 8\mathrm{H_2O} + 5\mathrm{I_2}\)

rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.stem:
(i) A black-brown coloured solid (A) when fused with KOH in the presence of air, produces a dark green coloured compound (B) which on electrolytic oxidation in alkaline medium gives a dark purple coloured compound (C). Identify (A), (B) and (C). Write the reactions involved.
(ii) What happens when an acidic solution of the green compound (B) is allowed to stand for some time ? Also write the equation involved. What is this type of reaction called ?
rows.solution:
(i) The colours identify the series. A black-brown solid that is the starting material for permanganate is manganese dioxide; fusing it with alkali in air oxidises manganese from \(+4\) to \(+6\) and gives the dark green manganate ion; electrolytic oxidation in alkaline medium takes it on to \(+7\), the dark purple permanganate.

\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{MnO_2}\), \(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{K_2MnO_4}\), \(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{KMnO_4}\)

\(2\mathrm{MnO_2} + 4\mathrm{KOH} + \mathrm{O_2} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{K_2MnO_4} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)
\(\mathrm{MnO_4^{2-}} \xrightarrow{\text{electrolytic oxidation in alkaline solution}} \mathrm{MnO_4^-} + e^-\)

(ii) The manganate ion is stable only in alkali. Acidify it and it does not survive: it disproportionates, some of the manganese going up from \(+6\) to \(+7\) and the rest coming down to \(+4\), so the green solution turns purple and a brown precipitate of manganese dioxide appears.
\(3\mathrm{MnO_4^{2-}} + 4\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + \mathrm{MnO_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)
Because the same element is both oxidised and reduced in one reaction, this is called a disproportionation reaction.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(i) Write the product(s) when :
(I) One mol of ethanal is treated with 1 mol of \(\mathrm{CH_3OH}\) in the presence of dry HCl gas.
(II) Benzaldehyde is treated with conc. NaOH.
(III) Ethanoic acid is heated in the presence of \(\mathrm{P_2O_5}\).
(ii) Write a simple chemical test to distinguish between Ethanal and Propanal.
(iii) Write the name of the reagent to transform Allyl alcohol to Propenal.
rows.solution:
(i)(I) One mole of alcohol adds across the carbonyl to give a hemiacetal; the second mole, which would take it on to the acetal, is not supplied.
\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO} + \mathrm{CH_3OH} \xrightarrow{\text{dry }\mathrm{HCl}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH(OCH_3)(OH)}\)

(II) Benzaldehyde has no \(\alpha\) hydrogen, so with concentrated alkali it undergoes the Cannizzaro reaction and disproportionates: one molecule is reduced to the alcohol and another oxidised to the salt of the acid.
\(2\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO} + \mathrm{NaOH\ (conc.)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2OH} + \mathrm{C_6H_5COONa}\)

(III) Phosphorus pentoxide is a dehydrating agent, and two molecules of the acid lose one molecule of water between them to give the anhydride.
\(2\mathrm{CH_3COOH} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{P_2O_5}} (\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

(ii) Use the iodoform test. Ethanal has the \(\mathrm{CH_3CO-}\) grouping, so warming it with sodium hydroxide and iodine gives a yellow precipitate of iodoform; propanal has an ethyl group next to the carbonyl and gives none. Both are aldehydes, so Tollens' reagent would not separate them.

(iii) Pyridinium chlorochromate, PCC. It oxidises the primary alcohol to the aldehyde and, unlike an acidified permanganate or dichromate, leaves the carbon-carbon double bond of the allyl group untouched, so prop-2-en-1-ol gives prop-2-enal.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(i) Draw the structure of the semicarbazone of acetone.
(ii) Why are \(\alpha\)-hydrogen atoms of aldehydes and ketones acidic in nature ?
(iii) Arrange the following compounds in increasing order of their reactivity towards HCN :
\(\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3CHO}\), \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-CO-CH_3}\)
(iv) Write the reaction involved in Etard reaction.
(v) Write the product when cyclohexanecarbaldehyde reacts with Zn(Hg)/conc. HCl.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — sub-part (v)'s reactant is DRAWN: a PLAIN hexagon (no inner circle, no double bonds, i.e. a cyclohexane ring) bearing —CHO, confirmed at 4x zoom. Named losslessly in the stem as cyclohexanecarbaldehyde, so the row is answerable from text and no collision is possible with a differently-drawn sibling; the reading is corroborated by the official marking scheme, whose answer is a plain hexagon bearing CH3 (methylcyclohexane, the Clemmensen product). Sub-part (iii)'s third compound is also drawn, but as a typeable condensed structure and is transcribed as \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-CO-CH_3}\). Page idx 18.
rows.solution:
(i) Semicarbazide condenses with the carbonyl group of acetone and water is eliminated, so the \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\) becomes \(\mathrm{C{=}N-NHCONH_2}\):
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{C{=}N-NHCONH_2}\)

(ii) The \(\alpha\) hydrogen is on the carbon next to the carbonyl group, which withdraws electrons strongly. When that proton is lost the carbanion left behind does not have to hold the charge on carbon: it is delocalised onto the electronegative carbonyl oxygen. The resonance stabilisation of the conjugate base is what makes the \(\alpha\) hydrogen acidic.

(iii) Reactivity towards \(\mathrm{HCN}\) falls as alkyl groups make the carbonyl carbon less electrophilic and more crowded. A tert-butyl group alongside a methyl hinders it most, two methyl groups moderately, and one methyl with a hydrogen least. The increasing order is
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C-CO-CH_3} < \mathrm{CH_3COCH_3} < \mathrm{CH_3CHO}\)

(iv) Etard reaction. Toluene is treated with chromyl chloride, which oxidises the methyl group to a chromium complex, and hydrolysis of that complex gives benzaldehyde without oxidising it further to the acid:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_3} \xrightarrow[\text{(ii) }\mathrm{H_3O^+}]{\text{(i) }\mathrm{CrO_2Cl_2}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CHO}\)

(v) Zinc amalgam with concentrated hydrochloric acid is Clemmensen reduction, which converts a carbonyl group all the way to \(\mathrm{CH_2}\). The \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) on the ring therefore becomes \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\), and the product is methylcyclohexane.

rows.stem:
(i) Calculate the electrode potential of a half-cell for zinc electrode dipping in \(0{\cdot}01\) M \(\mathrm{ZnSO_4}\) solution at 25°C.
Given : \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{Zn^{2+}/Zn}} = -\,0{\cdot}76\ \mathrm{V}\)
[\(\log 10 = 1\)]
(ii) Write anode, cathode and overall reaction involved in dry cell.
(iii) Equilibrium constant (\(\mathrm{K_c}\)) is related to \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{cell}}\), but not to \(\mathrm{E_{cell}}\). Why ?
rows.solution:
(i) For a single electrode the Nernst equation is written for the reduction half reaction \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}} + 2e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn}\), with the solid metal taken as unit activity:
\(E_{\mathrm{Zn^{2+}/Zn}} = E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Zn^{2+}/Zn}} - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{1}{[\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}]}\)
\(= -0.76 - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{1}{0.01}\)
\(= -0.76 - \dfrac{0.059}{2} \times 2\)
\(= -0.76 - 0.059 = -0.819\ \mathrm{V}\)

Diluting the solution below the standard 1 M has made the potential more negative, which is what it should do: less \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) present makes the reduction less favourable.

(ii) In a dry cell the zinc container is the anode and a graphite rod surrounded by manganese dioxide and carbon is the cathode.
Anode: \(\mathrm{Zn(s)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} + 2e^-\)
Cathode: \(\mathrm{MnO_2} + \mathrm{NH_4^+} + e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{MnO(OH)} + \mathrm{NH_3}\)
Overall: \(\mathrm{Zn} + 2\mathrm{MnO_2} + 2\mathrm{NH_4^+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} + 2\mathrm{MnO(OH)} + 2\mathrm{NH_3}\)

(iii) At equilibrium the cell reaction has no net direction left, so \(E_{cell}\) has fallen to zero. Putting that into the Nernst equation gives \(E^{\circ}_{cell} = \dfrac{0.059}{n}\log K_c\), so it is \(E^{\circ}_{cell}\) that fixes \(K_c\). This must be so: \(E_{cell}\) depends on the concentrations present at that instant and changes as the reaction runs, whereas an equilibrium constant is fixed for a given reaction at a given temperature — and only \(E^{\circ}_{cell}\), which is likewise fixed, can determine it.

rows.stem:
(i) The conductivity of \(0{\cdot}001\) M solution of acetic acid is \(3{\cdot}905 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}}\). Calculate its molar conductivity and degree of dissociation (\(\alpha\)).
Given : \(\lambda^{o}_{\mathrm{CH_3COO^-}} = 40{\cdot}9\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)
\(\lambda^{o}_{\mathrm{H^+}} = 349{\cdot}6\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)
(ii) Give reasons for the following :
(I) Why does a mercury cell deliver a constant voltage for its entire life ?
(II) Why is it necessary to use salt bridge in a galvanic cell ?
rows.solution:
(i) Acetic acid is a weak electrolyte, so its limiting molar conductivity cannot be found by extrapolation and is built up from the ionic values by Kohlrausch's law:
\(\Lambda^{\circ}_m = \lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{H^+}} + \lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{CH_3COO^-}} = 349.6 + 40.9 = 390.5\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)
(The marking scheme prints these two values in the opposite order to its own labels; the sum, and so the answer, is unaffected.)

The molar conductivity at this concentration comes from the measured conductivity:
\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{C} = \dfrac{3.905 \times 10^{-5} \times 1000}{0.001} = 39.05\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

and the degree of dissociation is the ratio of the two:
\(\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda^{\circ}_m} = \dfrac{39.05}{390.5} = 0.1\)

So only about one molecule in ten is dissociated at this concentration, which is what makes acetic acid a weak acid.

(ii)(I) The overall reaction of a mercury cell, \(\mathrm{Zn(Hg)} + \mathrm{HgO(s)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{ZnO(s)} + \mathrm{Hg(l)}\), involves only solids and a liquid. No ion in solution appears in the reaction quotient, so there is nothing whose concentration can change as the cell discharges, and the Nernst equation therefore predicts a potential that stays constant for the cell's whole life.

(II) The salt bridge does two jobs, and they are the same job seen from two sides. It completes the electrical circuit by letting ions move between the two half-cells, and in doing so it keeps each solution electrically neutral: without it, positive charge would build up in the anode compartment as metal ions are formed and negative charge in the cathode compartment, and that build-up would stop the reaction almost immediately.
